• Origin: South America
  • Growth rate: medium
  • Height: 3 - 5+ cm (average after two months in the tank)
  • Light demand: low
  • CO2 demand: low

• Common name: Amazon frogbit
  • Other names: West Indian spongeplant, South American spongeplant, smooth frogbit
  • Difficulty: easy
  • Lighting: medium to high
  • Optimal pH: 6.0–7.5
  • Water hardness: soft to medium
  • Temperature: 18–26 °C
  • Substrate: not needed
  • Growth rate: moderate to fast
  • Placement: floating
  • Height: roots can reach 30 cm or more
  • CO2: not needed
  • Propagation: through plantlets

Features:

  • Near-perfect round or circular shape.
  • Bright green, smooth, unmarked leaves.
  • Long, fuzzy, branching roots with fine trailing hairs, up to 50 cm.
  • Leaf width 1.3 to 7.5 cm.
  • Tiny, white, unisexual flowers.
  • Spongy aerenchyma tissue on the underside of the leaf (for buoyancy).
  • Rosettes of floating leaves lying on the water surface.
  • Seeds 1 mm long, ellipsoid and hairy.
  • Long roots serve as shelter for fry.
  • Young plants are produced through ramets/stolons.

When buying, the priority is a healthy plant. Look for:

  • Vibrant green leaves (avoid brown, decaying or yellow leaves).
  • Normal, healthy long roots.
  • Complete leaves without holes, rips or cuts.
  • No curls on the leaves.

It is a relatively cheap and popular aquarium plant available at most aquarium and pet stores, and can also be sourced online from reputable vendors.

Quarantine: Before putting them in the tank, quarantine or sterilize the plants (using bleach to get rid of parasites and treating with alum to eliminate snails).

  • They can carry parasites, pests such as snails, or even predators (dragonfly, damselfly nymphs, etc.).
  • They can be treated with chemicals (pesticides) to remove parasites, snails, etc. These chemicals are extremely poisonous to fish, shrimp and other invertebrates.

Amazon frogbit is native to Central and South America. It was first described in 1814 by the French botanist Louis Claude Marie Richard. The name comes from the Greek word 'limnobios', meaning 'dwelling in a lake'.

It has spread to freshwater habitats in Australia, Africa (Zimbabwe and Zambia) and North America (California), and is often considered an invasive species.

It is a floating aquatic plant in the family Hydrocharitaceae. The names 'spongeplant' refers to the spongy underside of the leaves, which increases buoyancy so the plant floats and moves with wind and water current.

Amazon frogbit grows in freshwater habitats with soft water and bright light. It is found in South and Central America, Africa, Asia, Australia and North America, in slow-moving freshwater: ponds, bogs, ditches, marshes and swamps. It spreads easily through seed dispersal and can adapt and thrive in a wide range of environments and water conditions.
The recommended minimum tank size is 40 litres. Amazon frogbit grows fast and can easily take over the tank. Nano tanks are not preferred; larger tanks accommodate it better.

Bèo tây Nam Mỹ là cây thả nổi, chỉ cần thả lên mặt nước chứ không trồng xuống nền. Loài này hợp nhất với bể hở, nhưng bể thường cũng nuôi đẹp. Bộ rễ dài và mảnh buông xuống trong nước, thành chỗ trốn cho cá sặc và các loài cá tầng mặt thích rễ cây nổi. Khi nước đủ phân và đèn đủ mạnh, lá mới sẽ vươn lên khỏi mặt nước, lúc đó có thể phải vớt bớt cho cây bên dưới còn chút ánh sáng. Nếu bèo bỗng lớn chậm hẳn lại thì đó là dấu hiệu nước đã cạn phân.

If there are enough nutrients in the water and the light intensity is good, new leaves will appear above the water surface. It may become necessary to remove some so that the plants beneath still get some light. When the nutrient level in the water decreases, it will grow much slower, which makes it a great indicator of the available nutrients.

Fertilizer: Amazon frogbit requires lots of nutrients to grow healthily. Supplement the tank water with a liquid fertilizer when necessary. However, if the tank has a high bioload from fish, snails and so on, external fertilization is not mandatory. If the plant shows no signs of deficiency, it should not need fertilizer.

If you keep shrimp, note that a high level of CO2 and copper (most fertilizers contain copper) is extremely dangerous to shrimp.

Planting: Do not submerge the leaves: water should not touch the top surface of the leaves, to prevent rot. Take care to avoid wetting the leaf surface during water changes and other maintenance.

Introduction to the tank: place the plants gently on the water surface. The roots submerge while the leaves stay buoyant, thanks to the spongy underside.

Care:

  • When the plants overwhelm the tank, remove some, to prevent the tank from becoming overcrowded and depriving other inhabitants of resources. The plant grows fast, as is typical of floating plants.
  • Trailing roots can be trimmed if they get too long, but do it gently, as the roots are fragile.
  • Take extra care during water changes to avoid submerging the leaves: leaves rot or turn brown when the top surface comes in contact with moisture.
  • Dose liquid fertilizer to boost the nutrient content of the water.

Problems:

  • Rot: a major problem, caused by the top surface of the leaves coming in contact with water. Keep the leaves dry.
  • Root breakage: the roots are very long and delicate, and sudden movements and strong currents can damage them.
  • Browning of leaves: caused by insufficient light. Increase the light intensity; affected leaves can also be removed, and new leaves will form soon.
  • Shading: Amazon frogbit can quickly overrun the aquarium, so it is better to keep it with plants that do not need much light.
  • Entanglement: the roots can become so long that they entangle with decorations, other plants or filters.

Temperature: Amazon frogbit lives in the tropics, so similar temperatures should be replicated in the tank: 18–26 °C. Colder water makes the plant grow slowly and stay small.

Hardness: It grows better in soft to moderately hard water; preferred hardness is 0–12 °GH.

pH: The optimal pH is 6.0–7.5. However, it is a pretty adaptable plant and tolerates a wider range of parameters.

Water flow: The plant likes slow-moving water. Fast currents might damage the plants, especially their long, delicate roots.

Lighting: Like most floating plants, Amazon frogbit requires moderate to high light. LED lights, full-spectrum T5 or T8 bulbs or fluorescent tubes can be used. Avoid very high-intensity light sources, as they can burn the leaves. Lighting duration should be 10–12 hours per day. It will not thrive in low light: it stops growing and becomes weak.

Substrate: Substrate is not a concern. The plant floats on the water without being submerged: the roots hang in the water while the leaves stay afloat. It gets all its nutrients from the tank water through its roots, not from the substrate, so any substrate can be used, whether gravel, sand, aquarium soil or another nutrient-rich substrate.

Filter: With a hang-on-back filter, surface agitation can push the frogbit around the tank. The solution is simple: create a 'roped off area' for the plant by stringing clear air tubing across the top of the aquarium. Keep the roots away from the filter so they do not get trapped and damaged.

CO2: The plant does not need CO2 dosing at all and does fine with naturally available CO2.

Amazon frogbit is compatible with plants that thrive in low light, such as Java moss, Elodea, Anubias, Vallisneria and Sagittaria. As a floating plant it blocks a lot of light from entering the tank. Avoid planting other floating plants alongside it to prevent overcrowding and competition for resources.

It can coexist with almost any freshwater fish: tetras, clownfish, bettas and gouramis are all compatible. Avoid keeping it with snails that nibble leaves and harm the undersides. Many reports say pond snails love to eat its tender leaves. Other snails such as ramshorn snails, nerite snails, Malaysian trumpet snails, Japanese trapdoor snails and mystery snails are not a concern.

It is considered one of the best plants for a shrimp tank, and any shrimp species can be kept with it.

It is a great choice for any aquarium with crayfish or crabs, which are plant-destructive invertebrates that eat and uproot everything in the tank. Floating plants like Amazon frogbit are the best choice.

Amazon frogbit is a flowering plant and reproduces sexually through flowers and seeds, but this is not viable in a home aquarium. In the aquarium it propagates vegetatively: mature plants grow smaller plantlets on ramets/stolons, which then detach, grow and develop into new plants.

Aquarium plant from tissue culture in closed cup. Limnobium laevigatum from South America is a decorative floating plant that is particularly suitable for open aquariums. It is 1-5 cm tall with leaves 5-15 cm wide. It is also good in traditional aquariums, because the fine, long and decorative roots provide protection to gouramies and other surface fish that like the roots of floating plants.

Benefits for the aquarium:

  • Removal of excess nutrients: like most floating plants, it helps remove excess nutrients and nitrates from the water. It grows rapidly and needs lots of nutrients to keep up.
  • Hiding and foraging spots: the long, fuzzy, trailing roots provide hiding spots for shy fish, and catch debris and detritus, making an excellent foraging place for fry and shrimp.
  • Aquascaping: it floats on the surface with long roots immersed deep in the water, adding a lot of green to the tank.
  • Shade/cover: it provides shade for fish and fry that thrive in darker environments, as well as low-light plants.
  • Filtration: its roots provide biological and chemical filtration, absorbing carbon dioxide produced by tank inhabitants and other detritus, keeping the water clean.
  • Algae control: it is very effective against algae, outcompeting algae for nutrients and suppressing its growth.
